questions.stem: What is a key characteristic of a Las Vegas algorithm?

options.text: It always produces the correct result.
It has a fixed running time.
It may produce incorrect results.
It does not use randomness.

questions.explanation: Las Vegas algorithms are designed to always produce the correct result. Their running time, however, is not fixed and can vary depending on the random choices made during execution.

distractorRationale.b: Las Vegas algorithms do not have a fixed running time; their running time is variable.
distractorRationale.c: Las Vegas algorithms always produce correct results; they do not produce incorrect results.
distractorRationale.d: Las Vegas algorithms do use randomness in their process.

questions.stem: Which of the following is true about Monte Carlo algorithms?

options.text: They have a deterministic running time.
They always produce the correct result.
Their running time is a random variable.
They do not use randomness.

distractorRationale.c: Monte Carlo algorithms have a fixed running time, not a random one.
distractorRationale.d: Monte Carlo algorithms do use randomness in their process.

questions.stem: Calculate the expected running time of Randomised Quicksort for an array of size 8. Provide your answer in $O$ notation.
questions.explanation: The expected running time of Randomised Quicksort is $O(n \log n)$. For an array of size 8, this evaluates to $O(8 \log 8) = O(24)$.

questions.stem: Why does Randomised Quicksort typically outperform deterministic Quicksort?

options.text: It avoids the worst-case $O(n^2)$ scenario by randomising pivot selection.
It always sorts in $O(n)$ time.
It does not use any pivot for partitioning.
It uses more memory to achieve faster sorting.

questions.explanation: By randomising the pivot selection, Randomised Quicksort avoids predictable patterns that can lead to the worst-case $O(n^2)$ running time, thus typically achieving better performance than deterministic Quicksort.

distractorRationale.b: Randomised Quicksort does not sort in $O(n)$ time; its expected time is $O(n \log n)$.
distractorRationale.c: Randomised Quicksort does use a pivot for partitioning, but it selects it randomly.
distractorRationale.d: Randomised Quicksort does not necessarily use more memory than deterministic Quicksort.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes the expected running time of Randomised Quicksort?

options.text: It is $O(n \log n)$ on average.
It is always $O(n^2)$.
It is $O(n)$ for all inputs.
It is $O(1)$ for small inputs.

questions.explanation: The expected running time of Randomised Quicksort is $O(n \log n)$ on average, due to the random selection of pivots which distributes the input evenly in most cases.

distractorRationale.b: The worst-case running time is $O(n^2)$, but this is rare due to randomisation.

questions.stem: If the probability of a Monte Carlo algorithm producing an incorrect result is 0.01, what is the probability of it producing a correct result?
questions.explanation: The probability of a Monte Carlo algorithm producing a correct result is the complement of the probability of producing an incorrect result. Therefore, it is $1 - 0.01 = 0.99$.

questions.stem: Explain the trade-offs between using a Las Vegas algorithm and a Monte Carlo algorithm.
markingGuide: Discusses the correctness guarantee of Las Vegas algorithms.
Mentions the variable running time of Las Vegas algorithms.
Explains the fixed running time of Monte Carlo algorithms.
Describes the probability of error in Monte Carlo algorithms.
questions.explanation: Las Vegas algorithms guarantee correctness but have variable running times, which can be a disadvantage if time constraints are strict. Monte Carlo algorithms have fixed running times, making them predictable in terms of performance, but they may produce incorrect results with a certain probability, introducing a trade-off between accuracy and predictability.

questions.stem: Which of the following is an advantage of using randomised algorithms?
